finding.claim: GET /invoice/<inv_id> has no authentication or ownership check, so any caller (including unauthenticated) can read any invoice by its id.
finding.source: Unauthenticated HTTP request with attacker-chosen inv_id in the URL path (invoices.py:7).
finding.sink: INVOICES.get(inv_id) at invoices.py:9 followed by jsonify(inv) at invoices.py:10 returns the full invoice record, including the customer field.

trace.note: Route registered with no auth decorator, no login_required, no role check.
get_invoice(inv_id) takes the id directly from the URL.
Looks up the invoice by id only. Does not compare inv['customer'] to g.user['id'] (unlike /my/invoice/<inv_id> at line 16).
Serializes and returns the whole invoice to the caller.

finding.guards_checked: Checked this file for decorators, before_request hooks, ownership comparisons and g.user usage. None guard this route. The sibling /my/ routes do ownership checks, which suggests this route is meant to be restricted, but nothing here enforces that. Caveat: if the deployed app registers a global before_request that requires login and does not run an ownership check, the finding is still valid, because that would only prove a caller is logged in, not that they own the invoice. No auth middleware is included in the repo I was given, so I could not rule out a deployment-level control that blocks this route entirely.

verdict.guard_found: none. invoices.py:7 registers the route with no decorator, invoices.py:9 looks up INVOICES.get(inv_id) with no ownership comparison, and invoices.py:10 returns the whole record. The file has no before_request hook, and g.user is read only in the /my/ routes (lines 16 and 23), where it is never set.
verdict.reason: The trace matches invoices.py:7-10: the /invoice/<inv_id> route has no auth or ownership check and returns the full invoice to any caller. The only open question is whether the deployment adds a global auth layer, which the repo does not include; if one exists that still lacks an ownership check, the finding stands.
